Saturated bars mark the six codes above 10% of conversations (dashed line) that the harness targets (§ 5.1 ); colours follow Figure 2 . Each percentage uses all 900 conversations as the denominator. Code definitions appear in Appendix B . Pairing each conversation with its teacher’s system prompt lets us identify where chatbots fall short. To this end, we build a failure mode taxonomy (§ 4.1 ), annotate all 900 conversations (§ 4.2 ), and analyze the results (§ 4.3 ) to inform the design of better educational chatbots. 4.1 Theory-backed Failure Mode Taxonomy We build the taxonomy deductively and refine it inductively: we synthesize failure categories from prior evaluation frameworks and refine them against observed data, following prior work on AI tutor evaluation. Our sources span educational AI evaluation ( LearnLM Team et al., 2024 ; Macina et al., 2023 ; Maurya et al., 2025 ) , learning sciences ( Chi and Wylie, 2014 ; Koedinger et al., 2012 ) , human–AI interaction ( Amershi et al., 2019 ) , and red-teaming Ganguli et al. (2022) . From tutoring datasets, we draw distinctions between diagnosis and remediation, scaffolding and feedback, and response length, consistency, and learner adaptation. Learning-science frameworks connect instructional choices to learning processes, information demands to limited processing capacity, and learner contributions to cognitive engagement, while human–AI interaction guidelines address capability expectations, correction, and context maintenance. Throughout, our coding relies on observable conversational evidence and the task-specific requirements in each teacher’s prompt. The resulting taxonomy (Table 3 ) organizes 29 secondary codes under four primary codes, each indexed by the initial of its category: Factual (7 secondary codes) failures occur when the bot gives wrong, incomplete, inconsistent, or ungrounded content, or oversteps the prompt’s boundaries, such as confirming a wrong derivative (F1) or grading against generic criteria instead of the attached rubric (F4). Workflow (9) failures occur when the conversation breaks down: questions go unanswered, output is broken or repetitive, or the prompt’s intended flow is skipped, such as ignoring a student’s question about the due date (W2) or opening without introducing what the bot can help with (W9). Diagnose (6) failures occur when the bot misreads the student’s prior knowledge, level, errors, or signals before or while responding, such as failing to diagnose a learner’s mistake in a calculation (D3) or repeating the same explanation after "I still don’t get it" (D5). Pedagogical (7) failures occur when the bot reveals answers early, over-scaffolds, mismatches strategy to task, or fails to engage the student, such as replying to a pasted problem with the full solution (P1) or asking Socratic questions about a definition the student only needs to look up (P2). Most codes derived from prior literature, with two (W7 and W8) emerged inductively from the data. Multiple codes can apply to a single bot turn; for example, answer dumping (P1) often co-occurs with no diagnosis before instruction (D1). The full definition and an example of each secondary code are given in Appendix B . Full definitions and examples are listed in Appendix B . 4.2 Annotation Method We used LLM-assisted coding, an approach increasingly adopted for large-scale qualitative annotation ( Ziems et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) . Two authors independently annotated two disjoint sets of end-user conversations with the 29 codes: an evaluation sample of 45 randomly selected conversations (5%), and an example pool of 10 further conversations. On the evaluation sample, they reached Cohen’s κ = 0.71 \kappa=0.71 pooled over all conversation–code pairs. They resolved disagreements through discussion to produce consensus labels and refined the codebook accordingly. We then built an annotation prompt for a GPT-5.6-Sol judge from the refined codebook and the 10 example-pool conversations as in-context examples. On the 45-conversation evaluation sample, none of which appeared in the prompt, the judge reached κ = 0.85 \kappa=0.85 against the human consensus labels. This exceeds inter-annotator agreement because consensus labels remove the individual disagreements that lower agreement between two annotators. We used the judge to annotate the remaining conversations. 4.3 Analysis We analyze failure prevalence across all 900 conversations and examine co-occurrences among codes from the four taxonomy categories. A conversation may contain multiple failures. Failures extend beyond incorrect answers. Missing required workflow steps (W7) is the most frequent failure (484 conversations; 53.8%), more than five times as common as incorrect content (F1; 10.1%), followed by absent expectation setup (W9; 301, 33.4%; Figure 1 ). The two codes co-occur in 232 conversations (25.8%). Within the Factual category, guardrail breaches (F5; 149, 16.6%) are also more common than incorrect content (F1; 91, 10.1%). These findings connect the Factual and Workflow categories through different aspects of teacher intent: F5 concerns explicit restrictions on the bot’s behavior, W7 concerns required instructional steps, and W9 concerns communicating the bot’s role and expectations to students. Their prevalence shows that following teacher-defined procedures and boundaries is a central challenge in these conversations, which answer correctness alone does not capture. Overload concerns both information volume and question pacing. Cognitive overload (P3) appears in 244 conversations (27.1%) and multi-question overload (W6) in 190 (21.1%). Both occur in 100 conversations (11.1%), while 234 have only one of the two labels. Overall, 334 conversations (37.1%) contain at least one form of overload. The distinction between these Pedagogical and Workflow codes identifies two demands on learners: processing information and responding to questions. P3 captures excessive content relative to the learner’s level or task, whereas W6 captures multiple questions posed in one turn, with students answering at most one and leaving the rest unanswered. Their partial overlap supports addressing information volume and question pacing separately: reducing response length alone may leave excessive questioning unaddressed. To address these failures, we design a harness — a prompt-level wrapper that runs around each teacher’s original chatbot, leaving the teacher’s prompt unchanged, with components that map explicitly to observed failure modes. We target W7, W9, P3, W6, F5, and F1, the six codes occurring in more than 10% of conversations (Figure 1 ). The harness has three components: a prompt for each target failure mode, an opening self-introduction, and persistent memory of teacher intent extracted by an LLM. Failure-specific prompts. Each prompt provides instructions for addressing one failure mode (Table 4 ). At each turn, these six prompts are combined with the original teacher prompt, cached teacher intent, and dialogue history to generate the next response (Figure 2 c). Opening self-introduction. Before the student speaks, the tutor introduces its role and scope and asks any opening question required by the teacher (Figure 2 b). This opening addresses W9 and becomes the first message in the dialogue history. Teacher intent memory. Before interaction, the bot’s tutor LLM extracts what the teacher expects the learner to do from the original teacher prompt (Figure 2 a). Each requirement is stored with a supporting quote in persistent memory and reused across turns. This memory supports W7: the tutor uses it alongside the dialogue history to identify completed steps and guide the learner through the remaining requirements. 5.2 Evaluation Study setup. We selected the ten chatbots with the most end-user conversations in EduWild and recruited U.S.-based students currently enrolled in college, including universities, community colleges, and associate degree programs, through Prolific 2 2 2 https://app.prolific.com/ . Participants were randomly assigned to one chatbot in either the control or the harness condition. Control chatbots were duplicates of the original Playlab chatbots. Harness chatbots used the same Playlab interface but routed each response through the harness pipeline, so the two conditions were indistinguishable to participants. Each participant read a one-sentence scenario describing the chatbot’s intended user, took on that role, and chatted with the chatbot for at least three minutes; the task took a median of 8 minutes. Participants received $3 after a team member reviewed the chat log, plus a bonus of up to $3 for deep engagement. The analysis includes 200 participants and conversations, 100 per condition. The study was approved by our institution’s IRB. The full task description is in Appendix D . Measures and analysis. We applied the GPT-5.6-Sol judge described in § 4.2 to both conditions. Our main outcome is the number of distinct target failure codes per conversation (F1, F5, W6, W7, W9, and P3; range 0–6). We also examine all 29 codes and the proportion of conversations with at least one selected failure label. We report averages with equal weight across bots and estimate 95% confidence intervals by bootstrapping participants within each bot and condition. All intervals describe the difference between harness and control; differences in prevalence are expressed in percentage points (pp). Individual-code intervals are pointwise. Table 4 reports the intervals. Overall reduction in failures. The mean number of distinct target failure codes decreases from 1.406 in control to 0.489 with the harness, a 65.2% relative reduction. Across all 29 codes, the mean decreases from 2.968 to 0.991. The proportion of conversations with at least one selected failure label decreases from 84.7% to 55.7%. Differences between control rates and corpus prevalence are discussed in Appendix D . Interaction load improves most clearly. All six target codes have lower observed prevalence in the harness condition (Table 4 ). Cognitive overload (P3) decreases from 39.7% to 7.6%, an 80.9% relative reduction. Multi-question overload (W6) decreases from 27.7% to 1.1%, a 96.0% relative reduction. These improvements address the content and question overload identified in our corpus analysis. Missing workflow steps (W7) decrease from 43.9% to 32.2% and remain the most prevalent target failure with the harness. Changes beyond the target codes. We also observe lower prevalence of unanswered student questions (W2), repetition loops (W5), ignored learner signals (D5), over-scaffolding (P2), and strategy–task mismatch (P4). Over-scaffolding decreases from 17.5% to 0.8%, alongside lower repetition-loop prevalence (17.8% to 2.8%). Early answer dumping (P1), however, increases from 6.0% to 9.8%. This trade-off mirrors Section 4.3 : instructions that curb over-scaffolding and question overload appear to push the bot toward giving answers sooner. It reinforces that the amount of help must adapt to the learner’s current state rather than shift uniformly in one direction. 6 Conclusion We introduce EduWild , a dataset of 1,726 real-world conversations with 217 teacher-configured educational chatbots, paired with the instructions behind them, and a 29-code taxonomy for analyzing their failures. Our analysis of 900 end-user conversations shows that failures to follow teacher-defined workflows and boundaries outnumber incorrect content, alongside frequent difficulties in managing interaction load and timing support. A harness targeting these failures reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation by 65.2% in a study with 200 participants, with the largest absolute reductions in cognitive and multi-question overload. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbot behavior. Limitations Our dataset comes from adult learners interacting with teacher-created chatbots on one educational platform. The participant study covers the ten most frequently used bots. Its participants role-played the intended user from a scenario card rather than pursuing their own coursework, so their motivation and behavior may differ from those of the real students in the corpus. Extending the study to other age groups, platforms, and classroom settings would help establish how broadly these failure patterns and harness benefits apply. Our annotation relies on a human-calibrated LLM judge. Some codes, such as cognitive overload and pedagogical mismatch, involve judgments about task demands and learner needs. Further human review and evaluation on a separate annotated sample would strengthen the assessment. Conversation-level labels capture the presence of a failure category, while its frequency and severity within a conversation deserve further study. We evaluate the harness through failures observed in conversations. Future studies should also assess learning outcomes and learner experience. Testing each harness component separately would help identify which components produce the observed improvements. Bots using the harness still miss required workflow steps. Early answer dumping is also more frequent in the harness condition. Future work should improve how the bot follows the teacher’s workflow and decides when to ask a question or provide an answer. Ethical Considerations Human participants. The corpus collection and participant study were approved by our institution’s IRB, with identifying details withheld for review. Educators and end users in the corpus provided informed consent for research use of their chatbots and conversation logs under the platform’s data use policy. All were adults, and end users confirmed that they were at least 18 years old. The Prolific study recruited U.S.-based college students and informed them that their interactions would be used to study educational chatbots. Participants received $3, with bonuses of up to $3 for deep engagement; the median task duration was eight minutes. Recruitment and task instructions appear in Appendix D . Privacy and data sharing. We replaced personal information with placeholders in transcripts and system prompts. Although corpus end users accessed chatbots through anonymous links without accounts, educational conversations and course context can still reveal sensitive information or enable indirect identification. Upon publication, we will share the de-identified dataset with researchers under a data use agreement prohibiting re-identification and commercial use, and release the codebook, annotation prompts, and analysis code publicly. Research consent does not by itself establish redistribution rights for third-party teaching materials; sharing such materials requires attention to their licenses and permissions. Educational impact and responsible use. Our work aims to help educators identify and reduce failures in educational chatbots. Incorrect explanations, misleading course guidance, excessive questioning, and premature answers can confuse learners or undermine independent work. Following teacher instructions more closely does not ensure that those instructions are pedagogically appropriate or free from bias. The harness still produces failures, and reduced failure labels do not establish improved learning or safe autonomous deployment. Use in education should therefore retain educator oversight, verification of consequential guidance, and a way for learners to seek human help. The codebook and LLM judge support analysis of chatbot behavior; their labels should not be used to grade learners or rank educators. Before broader deployment, evaluation should examine whether the harness serves learners with different language backgrounds, accessibility needs, and levels of prior knowledge.
